summary:
Victoria stands under Australia's national framework on gender identity. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. No Victorian or Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017.

Victoria's own anti-vilification machinery was rebuilt by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958 while repealing the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act, with the stated aims of equal participation and public safety. The Act carries gender identity as a ground but takes effect on 30 June 2026, and until that date Victoria's vilification coverage outside the federal layer extends only to sexual orientation. A visitor reporting gender-identity vilification in Victoria before 30 June 2026 therefore rests on the federal hate-crime offence rather than on state law.

Trans-specific mortality has been examined officially in the state. On 29 August 2024 ABC News reported that a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people. The state government said it was reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups said they would press for their implementation.
tangentialFactors:
Vilification coverage across Australia is uneven outside the federal layer: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. Victoria's position is therefore middling until its 2025 Act commences, and Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024 while New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Restrictions on gender-related care sit in other Australian jurisdictions rather than in Victoria. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, exempting existing patients; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, and a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research. A visitor passing through those states on a longer itinerary faces a different care environment from the one Victoria presents.

Detention practice elsewhere in Australia also differs from any assumption a visitor might carry. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process; the 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

The Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement of April 2024 is no longer reachable and the New South Wales Parliament bill document would not load, so those two items rest on the record held here rather than on a live page.
localsOnly:
The Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025 aims at equal participation and public safety for Victorian residents, and it consolidates vilification remedies by moving civil protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958 while repealing the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act. Residents seeking to understand the new scheme can refer to the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission's official factsheet explaining the changes.

The coroner's recommendations are directed at the state's own health system. The Victorian government is reviewing them and local advocacy groups intend to press for implementation, so residents who are trans or gender-diverse are the population whose care access the inquest addressed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Victorian rule governing the placement of trans prisoners in custody was located in the inventory; the only detention standards sourced here are Queensland's, which do not bind Victoria. Whether Victoria operates an equivalent placement policy, or a different one, is unresolved.

The inventory contains no Victorian restriction on puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones or other gender-related care for under-18s, and no Victorian confirmation that such care is freely available. Any statement about access to care in Victoria would be unsourced.

The implementation status of the Victorian coroner's recommendations is not settled: the state government said only that it was reviewing them as at 29 August 2024, and no later outcome is recorded here.
